strength: Nails the core insight (top 5 shades go short, held cartons are a cheap fix) and builds a whole dated plan inside the cash, with an honest customer message in our own voice.
mistake: The ₹1.187 crore total leaves only ₹1.3 lakh spare against freight and 15% rush-cost variance, which is thin for an ops lead to execute; also it doesn't give a per-shade-ready reorder trigger at shade level.
to10: A slightly larger contingency (say 3–4%) plus a per-shade reorder/stock-trigger sheet the ops lead can run Monday to Monday without asking.

strength: Very tight math per line (covers, buffers, reorder points) and a clean ₹4.07 lakh reserve with a documented pre-order wording; the Night-out kit is a smart way to move palettes.
mistake: Pre-order copy says 'ship by 10 December' while the plan says rush stock lands 7 December — a small inconsistency, and the reorder-point table (8 weeks on a 42-day lead) is a bit loose. Also the 25,000 rush figure is larger than the gap-driven need, eating cash that could buffer freight.
to10: Fix the ship-date wording, tighten the rush quantity to the real gap plus sale-week demand, and carry a small contingency line so the owner isn't caught by freight.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart against the 2.5 break-even, fixes the feed first, rebuilds the $240k split so it adds up, and shows a profit range with assumptions on every line.
mistake: The projected brand search range ($148k to $168k profit) is optimistic and the reserve rule adds a little complexity; the 2.26 blended non-brand figure is right but the table mixes brand Search and PMax brand in one row, which could confuse a fast reader.
to10: Tighter headings, a single clean non-brand vs brand profit bridge, and one line on how you will protect Claire's experience if the cut to broad terms shrinks reach.

strength: Very readable and on-voice, with the profit table by segment and a sensible feed diagnosis checklist (sale price, variant link, structured data).
mistake: The forecast oversells: base case claims profit ~$205,900 and ROAS 4.6 on a PMax line assumed at 2.6 without evidence, and brand search at 25 ROAS after moving budget is a stretch; it also sets PMax target at 2.6 then 3.0 in a way that risks relearning twice.
to10: A defensible expected-profit range (not a single flattering base case), a consistent 2.5 break-even test on every line, and a calmer, single-change PMax plan.

strength: Three fixes ranked by money saved with the working shown, and every message written in our voice with one button each.
mistake: Sales-kept figure (£75.7k–£129.7k) is a bit high relative to the modest refund-share move and could over-promise the owner.
to10: Add the SMS option on day 3 (cheap, higher open rate than email) and a small per-audience breakdown of which bra styles drive 'too small', so the fit-page work has a target.

strength: Six messages including a day-3 'nearly there' email+SMS and a delivered email with real bra-fit guidance, plus feeding size reasons back to product pages.
mistake: The 'up to £183,800 sales kept' from a 82%→65% refund move on all returns is not credible for an owner and muddies an otherwise sharp plan.
to10: Show the swap maths conservatively (only size-related returns, £58 partial) and commit to a single refund-share target rather than a wide 'up to' figure.

strength: Nails the data: pause back for 'no time' as the main save, clean exits for trip-over leavers who return anyway, 12-month switch for monthly payers, reminder for non-progressors, and honest revenue maths with a range and no-invented-discount discipline.
mistake: Trusts untested switch/reminder numbers as 9%/39% without flagging a holdout test or noting the switch's year-commitment risk explicitly; the 'other' text box sits oddly inside the save screen.
to10: Add a 10% holdout test on the old flow to validate the assumed rates, a one-line customer-facing reassurance that pausing won't lose progress, and a sharper build order with owners and dates.

strength: Strong copy in voice, a 'remind me before next trip' opt-in that fits the data, per-panel exact wording, and a 10% holdout test that O1 lacks.
mistake: Gives 50% off to 'switching to another app' — a reason with no evidence it responds to discount, and against the owner's brief to stop giving the blanket discount; also adds a 'smaller daily goal' offer with zero supporting data.
to10: Drop the discount on 'switching', replace the invented 'smaller goal' with data-backed options, and tighten the money model so discounted revenue is counted honestly and the range is stated.

strength: Ranked by tickets we can actually remove, with the working shown and a honest low/high range; the three articles are in our voice, answer first, and don't promise refunds we can't give.
mistake: The forecast leans on an arbitrary 25-50% assumption presented as the headline ('expect about 1,965 to 3,930'), which is a softer promise than it sounds, and merging is dismissed in one line rather than weighed.
to10: Tie each of the three articles to a measurable success signal (e.g. 'if "did this help?" for article 1 goes above 60%, we've paid for the writer's week') and add the search-term tagging as an explicit same-day fix alongside the in-app links.

strength: Every article is genuinely ready to publish, and it does the small things an owner notices: the two-currency path, the cancel-vs-refund distinction, the 'deleting the app doesn't cancel Pro' line, and adding the dead search terms to article 2.
mistake: The forecast is a single number (about 3,700) with shares that read as chosen to reach a headline; it gives a half-shares floor but not the honest range the brief asked for, and merging 'Recording a payment' is proposed on thin grounds when it's already 71% helpful.
to10: Give the forecast as a range with the same rigor as the rest, and justify each share against a real signal (current 'did this help?' rate for the article, in-app link reach) rather than judgement alone.

strength: Straight, confident answer on the 20% cut with the lifetime maths, plus a clean tier table that rewards the top 20 at 40%/12 months without raising cost across the board.
mistake: The 90-day window cost is left as a vague 'biggest cost, review at day 90' with only a per-10% rule of thumb, so finance may feel the biggest change is unpriced.
to10: Price the 90-day window concretely from the 58% miss figure, and give the 40%/12-month partner rate a tighter cost cap tied to new customers only.

strength: Says the uncomfortable part plainly (the window raises the bill, the switch month costs $52,500) and keeps one rate so nothing overpays the top 20, with a crisp day-by-day table.
mistake: Claims the rival out-pays us in year one while arguing the rate stays competitive; the 40% first-12-months rival is a real retention risk that the plan doesn't neutralise.
to10: A small, cheap retention lever for the top 20 (a modest year-one uplift or bonus) so the 40% rival can't peel off the 17 creator educators, and a number for how many customers the 90-day window newly credits.

strength: Ranks the fixes by money saved and gives clear cost and sales-kept ranges; the customer copy is strong, short and on-brand.
mistake: It has no proactive day-3 update, yet credits the new flow with 50% to 67% of day-3-to-5 ticket reductions; moving dispatch earlier and a day-5 late email do not fully cover that silent window.
to10: Add the day-3 'nearly there' email or SMS, pre-select swap for size reasons while keeping refund visible, and align the ticket savings with the messages actually sent.

strength: Directly fixes the silent day-3-to-5 window with a proactive email/SMS, and links the portal to size reasons with swap first but refund still visible.
mistake: The swap upside of up to £183,800 in sales kept is optimistic and may be read as cash saved; it needs tighter framing and a clearer net margin or item-cost note.
to10: Turn every estimate into a holdout-tested range, show realistic net sales kept after item and postage costs, and make the delivery-range and day-3 triggers exact.

strength: The forecast is broken out by cause, not topic: it separates Simplify-debts tickets from other balance tickets, puts a different, justified share on each, and carries the arithmetic all the way to dollars — and the three articles are genuinely publishable, with app and web steps and real cancellation steps for Apple and Google.
mistake: It proposes merging a 71%-helpful article ('Recording a payment') on no evidence of duplication, which risks breaking the one thing that works, and it leads with a single optimistic 3,743 / 21% number instead of a range I could defend upward.
to10: Present the forecast as a low-to-high range with each share tied to something in the data, drop or heavily caveat the merge, and add a short 'what to watch next month' so I can tell whether it worked.

strength: It answers the actual question in the first three lines — three articles, five links, 11% to 22% — then says plainly that nothing needs merging because the problem is findability, not duplication, and defends a conservative range that leaves currency and merging as upside.
mistake: It applies one flat 25%–50% band to three different mechanisms and props it up with a comparison that isn't quite right (50% is not below the 38% 'did this help' rate), and the restore article has no web steps even though the searches come from both.
to10: Differentiate the shares by topic with a sentence each on why, add splitwise.com steps to the restore article, and suggest the inline 'Balances are simplified. Why?' link on the balances screen rather than only the Help link.

strength: It nails the real story: top-5 matte shades run out about 30 Nov, the ₹38,400 re-carton buys four days of runway, and the whole plan fits inside ₹1.19 crore with a rush order landing 7 Dec and a standard order for January.
mistake: The 'one gap we cannot close' framing and the 1–8 Dec out-of-stock is a bit timid, and the palette clearance at 'no less than cost' on 1 February is a soft exit rather than a hard recovery deadline.
to10: Tighten the gap plan: state exactly how many units of pre-orders will be taken and cap them, and put a firm date and price floor for the glitter palette clearance.

strength: It quantifies the gap in rupees (₹25.6 lakh in lost sales), gives a usable reorder-point table with weekly checks, and turns the glitter and liquid lipstick into a Night-out kit with cost, margin and a clear-through trigger.
mistake: The pre-order wording says 'ship by 10 December' while the order table says rush lands 7 December and the table says sellout ~1 December — small inconsistency, and the 5,000-per-shade rush split average is loose when some shades sell far more.
to10: Fix the pre-order ship date to match the 7 Dec landing, split the rush order by actual shade sales rather than an average, and name the owner for the weekly reorder check.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart honestly, puts the feed fix first, and lands a $240,000 split that adds up with profit ranges rather than vanity ROAS.
mistake: The headline brand math mixes brand Search and PMax brand spend into one $26,700 line, which reads slightly muddled; and the title string at 106 characters runs long against the 70-character first-fold advice it gives elsewhere.
to10: Voice it in our words ("Made to walk, made to wash") rather than spreadsheet shorthand, and tighten the brand table so each line is clearly its own campaign.

strength: Reads like us: warm, plain, grade-7, with the customers' own lines in the search ads. The PMax-without-brand table is the clearest single exhibit either answer produced.
mistake: The projection is too rosy: brand Search rebuilt to $18,000 at an assumed ~25 ROAS and PMax at 2.6 put profit at $205,900, a 42% lift in 30 days that its own cautious case does not defend. It also folds the feed fixes into a tight list without the 'what changed on 21 October' diagnosis step.
to10: A defensible, conservative profit range with the working shown per line, and the Day-1 feed diagnosis spelled out as the first action with root-cause checks.

strength: Ranked fixes by money with working shown, honest ranges, and the five messages written short in our voice with one button each.
mistake: Message 3 keeps 'Tracking may show nothing for about 2 days' even though dispatch now fires at warehouse exit, which undercuts the fix and still tells the customer to expect silence.
to10: Tighten message 3 to drop the 'quiet tracking is normal' caveat, and pull the day-3 ticket savings and the refund-to-swap switch into the top table so the money story is obvious at a glance.

strength: Strong, specific bra-fit copy and the delivered message that helps with actual fit before anyone decides to return; six messages give good coverage.
mistake: The swap-first saving is overstated: it quotes 'up to £183,800 in sales kept' from a 65% refund share, which pulls the one number an owner would sanity-check out of line with the others.
to10: Bring the swap saving down to a believable range with the maths shown, and lead with the three fixes ranked by money like the brief asked, rather than starting from the cost table.

strength: Reason-matched offers with honest maths, working range, and a build order that leads with re-enabling the pause — exactly the plan I can hand to the product team.
mistake: The 'too expensive' split numbers (3,379 + 1,901) are asserted without showing the 64/36 split derivation, and the reminder-then-stay assumption (39% stay) is borrowed from the discount cohort without flagging it as a guess beyond assumption 1.
to10: Show the derivation for the plan-type split, add the measurement plan detail (holdout size and decision thresholds), and give the five test-and-learn guardrails for the first month.

strength: Most complete reason map and warmly worded copy that fits our voice; keeps a 50% offer only for switchers, and adds a smaller-goal option for people who already have reminders.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount on the 'switching apps' group where the data shows discounts don't work, and its kept-count for that group (67) quietly counts discounted people at full value and claims 12-month retention for an untested switch.
to10: Drop the switcher discount, reconcile kept-versus-value maths (discounted cohorts at £4.95), and add a concrete sprint build order with the pause rebuild first.

strength: Ranked by tickets we can actually remove, with full working on the forecast, a low-end scenario, and all three articles written answer-first in our voice.
mistake: The forecast bakes in optimistic shares (40%, 40%, 50%) as a single number, and the currency article is credited a partial-month saving even though it sits in week 2 with no in-app link; the Save/settle-up merge in step 5 is a small distraction.
to10: Give the forecast as a single defensible range with the shares justified against today's help rates, and show currency and merging separately as upside not counted.

strength: Clean, honest forecast given as a low-to-high band anchored to existing help rates, with currency and merging explicitly excluded so the number can only improve.
mistake: It claims nothing needs merging and keeps 'How balances work' as a separate article while adding a new one, which still leaves the 21,000-view page unanswered; the lower-bound 25% on Pro refunds may undersell the 80% who are simply told the wrong place.
to10: Resolve the duplication with the old balances article (rewrite or retire it), add the in-app balance-screen callout, and show the exact search-term plumbing for 'undo delete' so those 4,900 searches land.

strength: A straight, numbers-backed 'no' to the 20% cut, plus a plan that fixes the real pain points (90-day window, faster payouts) with a first-30-days timeline the one partner manager can run.
mistake: The partner tier's 40% first-year rate adds cost and complexity; a simpler perk-led tier might be cleaner, but it's a minor point.
to10: Nothing major; maybe a quick sensitivity check on the 90-day window cost and a note on how to phase it if cash is tight.

strength: Clear, plain-English decision with solid lifetime-value maths and a practical first-30-days table; the 'bad news, said plainly' section builds trust.
mistake: The 90-day window cost is underspecified—saying it will raise the bill but not estimating the extra $63k per 10% rise leaves finance without a number; also, the $25 minimum is a bigger change than needed and might invite fraud.
to10: Add a cost estimate for the 90-day window (like Output 1 does) and justify the $25 minimum against the $50 compromise.

strength: It brings back the pause as the main save, splits the reasons by plan and reminder status, and makes the money maths clear.
mistake: The upside range is not fully derived and leans on untested switch/reminder assumptions.
to10: Show the range calculation explicitly, add a small holdout test plan, and confirm the billing pause can be rebuilt before sprint start.

strength: It gives a very complete one-screen flow with exact copy, segment counts and build/test notes.
mistake: It keeps a 50% discount for switching-app leavers and adds unsupported offers like a smaller daily goal, which weakens the margin discipline.
to10: Remove or clearly test the unsupported 50%-off and smaller-goal offers, and make every retained group tie back to evidence and owner economics.

strength: The finance case is airtight and honest: 12.5% break-even, four top-20 partners wiping out the saving, the lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, $1,174 net vs $1,130), and a 'bad news, said plainly' section that admits the 90-day window raises the bill and faster payouts mean a $52,500 switch month. The perk table sums to exactly $40,000 and the 30-day plan has dates, owners and a Partner definition (25+ customers) that matches the data's '20 people' reality.
mistake: It leaves the top 20 on 30% while a named rival pays 40% in year one, and argues that perks and speed compensate without testing that with the 17 creator educators who could walk. The free-plan line ('up to 20 Partners') also sits oddly against the 25+ invite threshold, so the $12,480 could overshoot.
to10: A costed counter to the 40% rival (a capped first-year bonus or matched 40% for the top 20, with the exact cost and where it comes from), a quantified estimate of what the 90-day window will actually credit us from our own funnel, and a line confirming existing lifetime commissions are grandfathered.

strength: It closes the rival gap directly with a Partner tier at 40% for the first 12 months (costed at about $46,000), makes the sharp point that the cut breaks a lifetime promise, splits the base into core / active middle / the 2,260 who brought nobody, and gives a day-90 scorecard with real targets (42% credited toward 70%, 140 to 180 active affiliates). The sample affiliate email sounds like us.
mistake: The Partner threshold of 10+ paying customers contradicts 'named contact for every partner' with one manager and blurs the 20-person focus the data is begging for; the 15-day payout schedule also leaves almost no refund hold and is never reconciled against the 30-day hold argued elsewhere. Add the $46,000 tier cost and the window cost and the owner never sees one net number against finance's $210,000.
to10: Make Partner invite-only with a named-contact cap of about 25, fix the refund hold at 15 days, and put the tier cost, the window cost and the cash timing into a single cost line so the answer to finance is one number, not three.

strength: Names the Monday move (re-carton 6,400 units for ₹38,400) and lays out four dated POs inside the ₹1.2 crore with a reorder-point table ops can run weekly.
mistake: The pre-order wording promises 'we ship by 10 December' while the plan elsewhere says rush stock lands 7 December and the gap runs to about 8 December; the dates don't line up, and the 3,200-unit gap is called out but not fully reconciled with the 25,000 rush order math.
to10: Make every date consistent (sell-out, rush landing, ship-by date), show the shade-by-shade unit split rather than an average, and write the customer message in our exact voice.

strength: Tells the truth about the one gap it cannot close (1 to 8 December) and handles it exactly in our voice: pause ads, cap orders, open a pro pre-order for artists like Farah, and a 'back on 9 December, tap Notify me' message.
mistake: Leaves only ₹1.3 lakh spare, so freight or FX surprises could push it over the ₹1.2 crore; a slightly larger reserve would be safer.
to10: A little more cash headroom and a shade-level split for the top 5 so ops doesn't average across shades.

strength: Takes the 4.0 apart against a 2.5 break-even, puts the feed fix first, and gives a $240,000 split that adds up with expected profit, not just ROAS.
mistake: The brand search projection (about 25 ROAS, $455,000 value) is over-optimistic and sits badly next to the real 17.0; bolded ROAS of 2.6 for PMax also looks generous for a campaign it just called 2.03.
to10: Tighter, defensible forecast ranges tied to last month's actuals per line, plus a short stop/scale rule for weeks two to four.

strength: The profit framing is honest and self-checking: non-brand is 2.26 and losing about $20,000, the ranges are anchored to real per-line ROAS, and it flags that 'women's flats' at 1.2 may be partly the feed bug rather than trimming it blindly.
mistake: Proposes a 50/50 title A/B test over 14 days, which delays the full title rollout and adds a test the owner did not ask for; brand search doubling to $24,000 at a 90-100% retention assumption is also optimistic.
to10: Roll the fixed titles out fully rather than testing half, and tighten the brand Search assumption with a clearer fallback if impression share does not fill.

strength: Ranks the three fixes by money and writes every message in our voice with one clear button and honest date ranges.
mistake: The swap-first 'sales kept' figure (up to £183,800) is inflated and could set a false expectation in the room.
to10: Tighten the swap savings to a defensible number and note that swap users may already differ, so gains are measured against the hold-out.

strength: Opens with bad news and a first move this week, and its swap and ticket savings are the most defensible numbers in either answer.
mistake: Runs the fit-finder and post-delivery messages later than needed and leans on a 'running late' email rather than the cheaper day-3 nudge.
to10: Bring the fit check and delivered message forward and add a specific first-time bra buyer post-delivery fit message with the same urgency as output one.

strength: Brings back the proven pause as the main save, splits 'too expensive' by plan type, and does the money honestly with a range and the discounted rate applied to switchers.
mistake: The 'trip reminder' opt-in sits on the done screen where people have already left, so it will get few takers; and a 'Which app?' box on the last screen adds nothing to the save.
to10: Give a real test plan for the two untested offers (the 12-month switch and the reminder) with acceptance thresholds, and move the 'remind me before my next trip' into the confirmation email so it actually gets seen.

strength: Clean structure, clear per-reason panels with real prices, and a sensible 10% holdout test and logging plan.
mistake: It keeps the 50% discount for 'switching apps' (a reason the owner flagged as wasted margin, with no data behind it) and adds an untested 'smaller daily goal' offer, muddying the money while leaving the biggest gain sitting on a billing feature that is currently switched off.
to10: Drop the discount path and smaller-goal idea, keep the offer set to what the data supports, and add an honest range plus a first-month read on kept subscribers by reason.

strength: A ranked, ticket-driven plan with the three articles written in our voice, a forecasted range with visible working, and per-screen link changes — exactly the decision I asked for.
mistake: The forecast is a blanket 25–50% saved across all three articles with one assumption, which is thin; it also stops short of saying which numbers depend on the engineer's day landing in time, and skips the currency/merge items from the forecast entirely (it says so, but it undersells the currency gap as a lever).
to10: Per-article, justified save rates (like 40% for delete because it already helps 64% of readers) and a currency article drafted or at least scoped, with the in-app link timing built into the low/high range.

strength: Per-article save rates with a stated reason for each, plus the currency article counted in the forecast, and a bonus currency-relevant step in the link changes; the refund and cancel distinction is clear.
mistake: Item 5 merges "Recording a payment" — which is already 71% helpful — into a "Settle up" article; that's work for little gain and risks wrecking a good article, and it contradicts its own "already helpful" note. The forecast is a single point (3,700) with only a half-share floor, not a range.
to10: Don't touch the 71%-helpful article; give a proper low/high range with working like the other output, and show the currency forecast's assumptions more plainly.

strength: It answers the finance question head-on with lifetime maths, then puts the money and manager time exactly where the data points: the top 20 creator educators, the 90-day window and faster payouts.
mistake: The table formatting is heavy and a couple of sentences (the 3.55% each line) are a bit dense for a grade-7 voice; also the one-rate-for-all choice leaves the top affiliates without a visibly better rate versus the 40% rival.
to10: A cleaner, plainer layout with the three money numbers (lifetime value, break-even drop, switch-month cash) in a small side box, and one short sentence on why perks beat a higher rate for the top 20.

strength: Very readable and well structured, with a strong set of extra ideas (partner tier at 40% first year, first-customer bonus, partner kit, day-90 review) and a friendly voice that matches the brand.
mistake: It quietly creates a real cost: 40% first-year for Partners on top of a 90-day window and no clear cap, and the 31% first-year share maths is dense and easy to trip over; the plan also splits the top 20 across two focus groups rather than making them the whole point.
to10: Show the full cost of the Partner 40% tier against the $40,000 perk budget and the commission line, pick one number for the window rather than 'review at day 90', and keep the friendly voice while tightening the maths sentences.

strength: It perfectly weaves the customer personas and brand voice into the supply chain action plan, knowing exactly how to handle the inevitable stockout without compromising the brand.
mistake: Very minor, but it could have provided explicit reorder points for future planning to help the ops lead automate the next steps.
to10: It is essentially a 10 because it completely understood the assignment, from the math constraints to the marketing nuances.

strength: Excellent numerical breakdowns, including calculating the exact buffer math for the rush order and margin on the bundled kit.
mistake: The tone is a bit generic and largely ignores the customer personas (Tanvi and Farah) provided in the brief, missing an opportunity to tailor the stockout strategy.
to10: Incorporating the brand's bold, playful voice and actively using the provided customer insights to shape the marketing response during the stockout period.

strength: Exceptional technical Google Ads expertise. Calculating profit per PMax sub-segment, explicitly detailing platform toggles (URL expansion, auto-created assets, listing group exclusions), and brilliantly linking the feed error to the poor broad match performance.
mistake: Missed a chance to draft specific ad copy leveraging the exact customer quotes provided, instead just instructing to 'lead with comfort and washing.'
to10: Writing out the actual search ad copy and titles using the provided personas' exact words (e.g., 'eight hours', 'folds flat').

strength: Flawlessly applying the brand voice and provided customer quotes directly into the ad copy and title recommendations.
mistake: Lumping all non-brand PMax performance into one row in the primary profit table, hiding the specific financial wins and losses of the sub-categories at a glance.
to10: Including more advanced platform mechanics, such as explicitly excluding bags from PMax so they don't cannibalize the Standard Shopping campaign, and providing granular profit tables for all segments.

strength: Excellent grasp of the numbers and a very realistic approach to how many tickets and returns can actually be saved.
mistake: Missed the opportunity to give practical, actionable fit advice in the post-delivery message to help first-time bra buyers.
to10: Including specific bra fit guidelines in the post-delivery email and explicitly ranking the fixes by money saved at the top.

strength: Nails the brief entirely, especially by providing tangible bra fit advice ('loosest hook', 'snug and stay level') in the post-delivery email and smartly noting that the swap AOV will likely be lower since it's usually just one item.
mistake: None that stand out; it follows all guidelines and constraints perfectly.
to10: It is already a 10.

strength: Very clear breakdown of the data and straightforward exact screen copy for every user reason.
mistake: Assumed the new billing system cannot handle the pause feature, whereas the brief only stated it was never turned back on.
to10: More creative solutions for the edge cases (like users switching apps) and a plan to measure the changes via a holdout group.

strength: Incredible product instincts: keeping the discount solely for app-switchers as a price match, offering smaller goals to those already using reminders, and holding out 10% for a proper A/B test.
mistake: None. The exact unrounded math and deep understanding of retention made this flawless.
to10: It is already a 10. A masterclass in reading a business brief.

strength: Nailed the brand voice notes, including the specific required phrase, and directly incorporated the target search words into the article title.
mistake: Adding the search keywords as a visible 'Search words' line in Article 2 is slightly clunky for the user to read, rather than weaving them all into the title naturally or relying on backend tagging.
to10: Suggesting a specific UI tooltip or line of text to add to the app screen alongside the link, to prevent the confusion before they even click.

strength: Very detailed ticket forecasting with clear, logical assumptions for the share of tickets avoided in each specific category.
mistake: Completely missed the specific brand voice instruction to include 'Here's who owes what, and why', and combined multiple tasks (refunding and cancelling) into one article.
to10: Following the explicit brand voice phrase instruction, keeping strictly to one task per article, and using the exact user search phrases in the article title rather than just backend tags.

strength: Correctly realized that a commission rate bump is too expensive and used the $40k perk budget to build a highly targeted top tier instead.
mistake: Missed the ethical and trust issue of retroactively cutting rates on 'for life' customers, which would destroy affiliate trust.
to10: Include the insight about how a retroactive rate cut breaks a 'for life' promise to existing affiliates.

strength: The brilliant insight that cutting commission to 20% on existing customers breaks the 'for life' promise we made to them.
mistake: Proposed a commission rate increase for top partners that would cost an extra $46k a year, missing my goal of rewarding them without raising across-the-board costs.
to10: Stick to the 30% flat rate for all tiers and use the perk budget to create the Partner tier, rather than adding a $46,000 commission liability.

strength: Rock-solid arithmetic that honors the budget ceiling, nails the 2.5x sale demand spike, and provides a clear mathematical reorder point formula.
mistake: Overlooks the specific persona dynamics from the brief, particularly Farah the bridal MUA who needs bulk shade security before December.
to10: Incorporate specific tactics for high-volume bridal makeup artists and ground the customer-facing tactics in our buyer personas.

strength: Brilliantly connects the stock math to customer psychology by creating a pro pre-order for bridal artists like Farah and order caps so Tanvi doesn't get shut out.
mistake: Left only ₹1.3 lakh as a cash buffer, which leaves very little room for sudden logistics or freight variance.
to10: It is already virtually flawless, but adding explicit SKU-level reorder point trigger formulas like Output 1 did would make it unbeatable.

strength: The opening profit breakdown against the 2.5 break-even immediately exposes why profit felt low despite the blended 4.0 ROAS.
mistake: Does not explicitly mention removing bags from PMax listing groups when scaling the Standard Shopping bags campaign, which risks internal cannibalization.
to10: Add negative keyword / listing group exclusion mechanics for bags in PMax, and include specific stop-loss rules for week two.

strength: Deep tactical mastery: removes bags from PMax listing groups to avoid campaign conflict, bundles PMax changes into one edit to limit relearning, and includes practical stop rules.
mistake: Title example at 106 characters runs slightly long for Google Shopping preview limits on mobile, though core keywords are well front-loaded.
